titleStmt.title: Filtering by Form: A User Study of Genre in a Digitised Historical Newspaper Collection

dhq:bio.p: Karin Stahel is a doctoral candidate and teaching assistant in Data Science and Digital Humanities at the University of Canterbury. Her research explores the use of machine learning algorithms to classify the genre of articles in historical New Zealand newspapers, with a particular focus on the use of interpretable methods.

dhq:abstract.p: The idea of genre as a useful search facet for large digital collections has received considerable interest, especially in relation to the classification and retrieval of web documents. However, while the idea of being able to filter a large collection to retrieve (or exclude) certain types of documents is appealing, in practice it is difficult to implement, particularly when an agreed classification scheme does not already exist. This paper explores how users of a large digitised historical newspaper collection, the National Library of New Zealand’s Papers Past (https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/), use existing keyword search and content filtering options and how they perceive genre and topic in the context of historical newspaper articles. The results reveal the variety of ways in which genre is interpreted, along with how it is understood in relation to topic. While the results show that a consistently shared conceptual understanding of genre does not exist among users, several examples are given of how the ability to filter by article type, particularly in combination with keyword or topic-based filters, would help users to identify articles of interest in digitised historical newspaper collections.

dhq:teaser.p: This paper explores how users of the National Library of New Zealand’s Papers Past collection use existing keyword search and content filtering options and how they perceive the concepts of genre and topic in the context of historical newspaper articles.

div.head: Filtering by Form: A User Study of Genre in a Digitised Historical Newspaper Collection
Introduction
div.p: The success of a library or archive’s digital initiatives, such as newspaper digitisation programmes and online interfaces, ultimately depends on their value to the most important stakeholder group, the users . However, understanding what is valuable is complicated by diverse user expectations, experiences, and levels of computer literacy . This study focuses on a digitised historical newspaper collection, the National Library of New Zealand’s Papers Past (https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers). The user experience of the existing interface is explored, along with perceptions of genre as a possible search facet and how genre is understood in comparison to topic.

Genre has long been considered a useful facet for information retrieval in large digitised collections and has been the focus of several classification studies using digitised historical newspaper datasets (examples: ). However, few studies have specifically addressed genre in the context of enhancing the retrieval of articles from a digitised historical newspaper collection (one example: ). The reason for this gap may be that genre relies on a shared understanding and expectations of the form and function of a text and, while we may intuitively recognise individual genres, they can be challenging to define . This becomes even more complicated when our goal is to define and apply historical genres for use by a modern audience. As Blankenship and Cordell point out, Nineteenth-century newspapers, in particular, challenge twenty-first-century understandings of genre. Nineteenth-century newspapers are densely packed with information, often with little delineation between texts, topics, or genres . In addition, the successful development and application of a classification scheme is contingent on that scheme being understood and accepted (at least enough for it to be practically useful) by the intended users . This leads to the questions addressed by this study: who uses the Papers Past newspaper collection, what do they search for, and how do they understand the concepts of genre and topic?

div.head: Previous online cultural heritage user research
div.p: The question of who uses digitised cultural heritage collections and why has been the focus of several studies. Many of the methods used in these studies, such as online surveys, web analytics, and interviews have also been used to explore user perspectives of genre, particularly in relation to web genres (for example the collection of studies in: ).

In the cultural heritage domain, user studies generally seek to characterise different user groups and understand their research practices and how they interact with digital resources. Studies undertaken in the last ten years include Bogaard et al., who analyse web query logs from the National Library of the Netherlands’ Delpher (https://www.delpher.nl/) platform to draw connections between users’ interests and related patterns of search activity . Borlund et al. use questionnaires and interviews to identify the users of three audiovisual archives in the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, and France, and better understand their information needs and search strategies . Clough et al. sample 240 search requests from users of the Europeana (https://www.europeana.eu/en) platform and use qualitative content analysis and mode/facet analysis (following ) to identify the types, subjects, and motives of user searches . Coburn explores historians’ attitudes towards digital collections and research practices in a case study based on semi-structured interviews with three library professionals and five academic faculty members at Newcastle University . Crymble analyses and compares the information retrieval behaviours of surveyed academic, genealogical, and casual users of British History Online (BHO) (https://www.british-history.ac.uk/) . Gooding combines semi-structured interviews, online surveys, citation analysis, and web log analysis to gain detailed insights from library staff and users regarding the impacts and challenges associated with digitised historical newspaper collections in the United Kingdom . Pfanzelter et al. collate feedback from separate surveys of users of the digitised historical newspaper interfaces of the national libraries of Austria, Finland, and France and discuss it alongside findings from direct testing of the interfaces by a team of digital humanities researchers . Their purpose is to explore the functionality and effectiveness of interface tools for different user groups and highlight areas where improvements could be made to enhance transparency and better meet the needs of researchers. Together, these previous studies provide a representative picture of the research methods typically adopted for digital cultural heritage user studies along with the types of data gathered, and they informed the design of the study described here.

div.head: Defining article genres in historical newspapers
div.p: The term genre means different things in different contexts, and even scholars in the same field do not necessarily agree on its scope or definition . In terms of newspaper articles, Ljung notes that while the category of news has been well studied by researchers in linguistics, sociology, and media studies, other types of articles such as obituaries, feature articles, and reviews have received little interest . Liddle describes the problem of defining and identifying genre in historical newspapers, even given the ability to quantitatively analyse these sources at scale:

Basic, seemingly intractable questions remain: How can scholars know a genre when they see one? What clues or markers should count as evidence for a genre's existence? Did discourse genres exist before being named by their original practitioners? Did they exist even if they had never been named? Simply defining the conceptual language we need for the rigorous study of genre may present the same kinds of difficulties faced by scientists who attempted to describe speciation before the discovery of DNA .

This study does not attempt to define a fixed terminology for the article genres that can be found in Papers Past newspapers, or even to argue the distinction between a genre and a topic. The term genreis simply used here to refer to the type of article (for example a letter to the editor or a notice), while topic refers to what the article is about .

As mentioned above, many of the methods adopted in cultural heritage user studies have also been applied to study user perceptions of genre as a facet for information retrieval. In their discussion of a research agenda for investigating the use of genre for information retrieval, Crowston and Kwasnik recommend an initial descriptive phase in which the terminology and sense of genres of a set of users is investigated . This is the first step in defining the set of meaningful labels which effective faceted search relies upon .

Because genres are socially constructed, different users will bring different expectations and requirements to their interaction with a genre-based search . Bowker and Star explain how one person’s noise may be another’s signal , and so it is inevitable that various interpretations are possible for any given set of genre categories. In addition, a meaningful set of categories must make sense when the genres are considered in relation to each other because we know what something is by contrast with what it is not .

The starting point for discussion and analysis of newspaper article genres in this study was to develop a list of article types which could potentially be found in Papers Past newspapers. The newspapers collection is just one of the digitised full-text collections available on the Papers Past website . The other collections include magazines and journals, letters and diaries, parliamentary papers, and books. The list came from an inventory of terms used to describe newspaper article types (variously described in the source material as types, categories, genres, and registers) compiled from the tags and filters already used in digitised online historical newspaper collections, published research on newspaper article genres (and some web genre literature), and controlled genre vocabularies or schema (see Appendix 1: Genre inventory for the sources and terms). Using a spreadsheet, the collated terms were separated into genre and topic, and similar terms (e.g., Readers Letters’ and Letters to the Editor) were grouped under a standardised label (e.g., Letter). This standardised label was almost always obvious as a common word or singular form (although singular was not always appropriate, as in the case of comics or amusements). This is similar to the approach taken by Ljung in his comparison of text categories in The Times (of London) and The New York Times, where he noted, the variety can be greatly reduced by subsuming the raw categories under a number of more general headings based on content and to a certain extent also on function . Examples of the original and standardised terms are shown in Table 1.

div.head: User survey method
div.p: The purpose of the user survey was two-fold. The first goal was to elicit user feedback on why and how they use the Papers Past newspaper collection, their perspectives of the interface and search options, and ideas for improvement. The second was to explore how users understand the concepts of genre and topic in the context of historical newspaper articles. The survey was not intended to be representative of the entire Papers Past user population, but rather to provide in-depth insights from an actively engaged group. Hence, a snowball sampling method was used to recruit participants, in which an initial target group were contacted and invited to share the survey via their networks .

The survey included a mix of open and closed questions, scales, and examples of Papers Past articles delivered via the Qualtrics platform (https://www.qualtrics.com). A pilot survey with seven post-graduate students and University staff was carried out to test the design and clarity of the questions. The responses to the pilot survey were anonymous and the feedback was used to improve the survey design before final distribution.

The final distribution list was developed in discussion with National Library of New Zealand staff, a digital humanities subject librarian, and academic contacts, along with internet research. The list was constructed using publicly available contact details for the individuals and groups identified, which included academic and professional historians, genealogists, authors, archaeologists, historical societies, and museums. The survey ran from 16 October to 22 November 2024. It was sent to 190 individuals and 47 organisations, and shared via a New Zealand libraries mailing list. In line with the snowball sampling approach, the targeted participants were invited to share the survey with their networks, which they did through newsletters, websites, and social media.

The survey was confidential and anonymous unless a participant chose to register their interest in receiving updates about the research. Where participants did provide their email address, this was stored separately from their other survey responses. The research was approved by the University of Canterbury Human Research Ethics Committee (ref: 2024/40/LR-PS) and participants gave informed consent.

div.head: Results
div.p: Following a screening question which asked if the participant had ever used Papers Past as a research source, including for personal or family research, 200 of the 203 total survey respondents continued to answer additional questions. As it was not mandatory for participants to answer every question, the number of responses to each is indicated in the following discussion and in the captions of tabulated results and figures. The median time taken to complete the survey was 41 minutes. Most of the respondents (98%) were from New Zealand and just over half (52%) were aged over 60.

div.head: Who uses Papers Past newspapers and why?
div.p: The survey participants were asked to describe their primary role when using Papers Past. Following a similar approach to Clough et al. , examples of the expected answer type were included in the question (e.g., professional historian, genealogist, family history researcher, author, student etc.), but the free text response format enabled participants to provide their own description. The answers were manually coded by the author using the Text iQ feature in Qualtrics, which allows topics to be assigned to text responses in order to categorise common themes. In this case, the topics were the types of roles described in each response. For example, the response casual user, mainly family history is tagged with Family history research and General/personal interest. This allows for a more fine-grained analysis of how participants describe their research roles, and the identification of frequently co-occurring roles. Figure 3 shows individual roles (where a respondent only described a single role) alongside the top 20 multiple role combinations. Family history research was the most popular single primary role, stated by 22% of respondents. In total Family history research was a focus, either alone or in combination with other roles, for 35% of respondents. Professional historians (13%) and genealogists (8%) were the next two most significant categories overall. The results align with the findings of previous user research on digital archives and newspaper collections. For example, the groups most significantly represented in Gooding's study of digitised historical newspaper collections in the United Kingdom are academic historians and non-academic genealogists and family historians . Similarly, Crymble identified the main BHO users as academic historians, genealogists, and casual users .

figure.head: The primary roles of respondents (n = 196). The left-hand chart shows the 14 single roles (as coded) and the right-hand chart shows the top 20 multiple code roles. The charts are mutually exclusive.
figure.figDesc: Two bar charts showing the primary roles of respondents (n = 196). The left-hand chart shows the 14 single roles (as coded) and the right-hand chart shows the top 20 multiple code roles. The charts are mutually exclusive.

div.p: Participants were then asked to describe their main focus or area of interest when using Papers Past, including geographic regions and time periods if relevant. The 190 responses reveal the broad interests of Papers Past users from family history, to finding political cartoons, to researching New Zealand’s relationship with Latin America. To identify general themes amongst these areas of interest, the responses were again coded. This time, the categories used were based on the mode/facet analysis described in Clough et al. . The category Article genre was added and applied where respondents mentioned a specific article type, such as letters to the editor, family notices, or reports, as in the example below:
My main focus/area of interest when using P/Past is content (letters to editor, public meetings, parliamentary reports, council meetings, opinion pieces, etc) relating to ... [topic and time period].

A code for Specific newspaper/publication was also added. Responses such as my family, my ancestors, whānau, or whakapapa were coded to the Specific person/group category. New Zealand, although a named location, was in this case considered to be a general location in terms of a Papers Past search, unless it was modified by a more specific term or used in the context of a more distinct geographic focus such as, music history of New Zealand and Australia, c. 1850-1980. The coded results are shown in Figure 4.

figure.head: The primary focus of respondents (n = 190). The left-hand chart shows all single focus responses and the right-hand chart shows the top 20 multiple focus responses. The charts are mutually exclusive.
figure.figDesc: Two bar charts showing the primary focus of respondents (n = 190). The left-hand chart shows all single focus responses and the right-hand chart shows the top 20 multiple focus responses. The charts are mutually exclusive.

div.p: Most participants search Papers Past with a specific focus, usually a person or group of people (such as a family or an organisation). They also search for specific locations and within specific time periods. A general topic or subject alone was the focus of around 5% of respondents, but 26% mentioned these in combination with other facets such as a specific location. In comparison, in Clough et al.'s study, general topical search was the largest search category (47.1%) . An article genre alone was the search focus of only 1% of the Papers Past respondents but overall 13% mentioned a genre focus in combination with other facets. This suggests that while genre alone is not often a focal point, it can be a means to an end; a part of the information need but not the main part. Of course, as it is not currently possible to filter a search by genre (beyond three high-level content types, Article, Illustration, or Advertisement, which are identified at the digitisation stage), a focus on specific article types is not likely to be top-of-mind for participants responding to this question. The responses point towards a genre filter being useful for a subset of users, but it should be integrated with existing filter options to provide flexibility for a range of use cases.

div.head: Search practices, preferences, and ideas for improvement
div.p: Keyword search and basic metadata filters are now standard features of most digitised historical newspaper interfaces but advanced options, including article type filters, are less common and more varied in their implementations . In the surveys analysed by Pfanzelter et al., the users of digitised newspaper collections were satisfied with basic search functionalities, aware of the limitations of the interfaces, and had many ideas for additional tools and improvements . For this study, understanding how Papers Past users search, and where they encounter limitations, was important to provide supporting context to their perspectives on genre and topic as search facets. Figure 5 shows the main Papers Past newspapers search interface as it appeared at the time of the survey.

div.p: Previous research, including Bogaard et al. and Sumikawa et al., found users of online library or other cultural heritage collections tend to make limited use of more advanced search options and that they can find such features difficult to understand . This is also the case for Papers Past, based on the responses to a question which asked participants to rate how often they used the different search and filter options (Table 2) . As expected, a simple keyword search is used often by most of the respondents (97%). Filtering by date (92%) and region (80%) are also frequently applied approaches, while filtering by newspaper title and by content type are used either sometimes or frequently by a majority of respondents. More than 70% of respondents said they never use the filters to limit searches to the most recently added content or the Ngā Tānga Reo Māori collection only, or made use of proximity search.

div.p: The limited uptake of more advanced search and filter methods aligns with the findings of other historical newspaper interface user studies. However, it is notable that the majority of participants do apply the existing basic content type filters for Article, Advertisement, or Illustration either frequently or sometimes, with 44% frequently using the Article filter. This indicates a need to focus searches on relevant article types and remove noise from results, but the functionality of such tools must be clear and intuitive in order to be widely adopted.

When specifically asked what they liked or found useful about the current newspaper search and filter functionality on the site, more than half of the 181 respondents mentioned that time period filters were useful (55%), followed by filters for region (28%), and newspaper title (9%). The ability to restrict a search using the exact words filter was identified as useful by 14% of respondents, although only 4% mentioned the equivalent ability to use Boolean search. Eight participants specifically mentioned the keyword search functionality as a positive feature. Thirty-three participants (18%) highlighted simplicity, ease of use, or the intuitive nature of the current interface as a positive, and of 145 responses to a subsequent question about new features, 37 participants were happy with the current functionality or simply said keep it simple. Some respondents acknowledged that they were not fully aware of existing functionality and suggested better guidance on using the available search features would be beneficial, for example through a video tutorial or more accessible hints and tips resources. Several respondents mentioned they would like more metadata, such as the date newspapers were digitised or added to the collection.

Pfanzelter et al. noted the users in their study found optical character recognition (OCR) errors to be a nuisance, and these types of inaccuracies were mentioned in 9% of the 164 responses to a Papers Past survey question about dislikes in relation to the current search and filter functionality . However, not everyone has issues with OCR. One participant commented:
I particularly like how good the OCR engine works. It almost always gets the text correct. Only occasionally do I find that asking the question with different words gives me what I am searching for.

Several participants mentioned that they liked the recently added OCR text correction functionality, but further improvements to the quality of the OCR text were also requested. Some noted the potential value of AI for correcting OCR errors and for enhancing search functionality. For example:

The ability for people to now make text corrections is a huge plus. I suspect that AI will be able to correct bad OCR text before long which could clean up almost all the errors. It would be fantastic to be able to filter out irrelevant results, e.g. if the family surname is Broad, it would be great to be able to filter out all the articles that mention broad beans, Broad Street, Broad Bay, etc. This sounds like another job for AI.

Several participants suggested improvements to name-based searching to allow proper nouns to be distinguished from other words with the same spelling (for example surnames such as Brakes, Lodge, or Walker). Filters that would enable search for short and common terms such as Te in Māori place names or a person's initials were also proposed. One participant suggested a two-tier search function, starting with all words and then being able to perform an exact phrase search within that cohort of articles.

Participants also highlighted the problem of identifying suitable search terms when spelling or language use had changed over time, or when multiple transliterations exist for Māori words, for example:
It does not take account of differences in old spellings e.g Chiffonier is more often found as ’cheffonier’, Kauri is often cowdie or kowrie.

Some of the feedback expressed as dislikes in relation to the current search and filter options or as suggestions for new features related to functionality which is already available, such as Boolean and proximity search and the ability to remove search term highlighting from results. Other participants suggested improvements such as being able to bookmark results, save searches, export text or PDF images of multiple selected results, or have access to more advanced citation options. There were also requests for a more recent and wider range of newspaper titles. Only seven participants (4%) said they disliked seeing repeated or duplicate articles or advertisements in the results.

While the quantitative data reveals limited uptake of advanced search and filter methods, the open-ended responses included many ideas for improvements such as more fine-grained date and location filtering (e.g., the ability to filter by day of the week) and the ability to visualise search results with maps or word clouds. Some respondents mentioned the current content-type filtering did not seem to work well, while others said they would like more options for filtering by article type or broader topics, supporting the idea of genre and topic as complementary search facets. For example:
I would like to see broad classifications: eg Family Notices, similar to Trove.

Not possible to filter with the Articles category. It would be nice to be able to look at Shipping only for example. Shipping is a common article sub category. It would also be nice to be able to filter out all the sports articles.
More subcategories within Articles category in Newspapers. I think I would get a lot more use out of Papers Past with that change.
An article category filter such as that used on Trove could allow you to filter for family notices and advertisements etc.
Would be great to have some categorising of the content of the newspapers e.g., obituaries, death notices, court matters and so on (probably a massive ask).

These responses illustrate how the existing content type filters (Article, Advertisement, Illustration) are too broad for the needs of some users, with survey participants particularly emphasising the need to further subdivide the Article category. Family notices (births, deaths, and marriages) were the most frequently requested subcategory. Other article types specifically mentioned as being useful to filter for included shipping lists, obituaries, court reports, sports articles, land records, and letters to the editor. These responses, taken together with similar feedback expressed under dislikes in the previous question, provide further support for the value of an article genre filter for Papers Past users.

div.head: Genre and topic in historical newspapers
div.p: The final part of the survey explored the participants’ understanding of genre in more depth, starting with a question that asked for comments on what the concepts of genre and topic meant to them, specifically in the context of historical newspaper articles, and how genre and topic were the same or different. There were 141 responses to this question. Some participants said they did not understand the difference, that genre and topic meant the same thing, or that they had never considered the distinction. Table 3 shows a selection of representative responses from those participants who made a distinction between genre and topic. There was general agreement that topic referred to the subject or theme of an article, but more variety in the interpretation of genre. Some respondents considered genre to be a literary, music, or art related term and were not sure how it applied to newspaper articles. Most respondents felt that genre was the broader or higher level concept, although a couple stated that topic was broader than genre. Around 36% of the respondents described genre in a way that aligns with the concept of a type of article, such as an editorial, a letter to the editor, notice etc. Several respondents pointed out that there could be considerable overlap between genre and topic.

div.p: In a follow-up question participants were specifically asked to consider genre, in the context of newspaper articles, as being the type of article as opposed to what the article is about. Given this context, they were asked to list up to six genres they might expect to find in a newspaper published in New Zealand in the nineteenth or early twentieth century. An additional free text field allowed respondents to comment on each genre and its potential usefulness for their research. A total of 360 genre entries were provided. These were manually reviewed and separated into genres and topics, which were then coded using the standardised set of terms from the genre inventory described previously. For example, Court reports was separated into Report and Court, and Births, deaths and marriages or Hatch, match, despatch [sic] was separated into Notice and Family. Figure 6 shows the 24 genres identified by respondents (using the standardised terms). Figure 7 shows the 33 topics that were mentioned more than once from 75 unique topics (again using standardised terms).

div.p: Comments regarding the usefulness of the identified genres (and topics) were extremely varied and more than anything reflect the diversity of research interests of Papers Past users. As would be expected from the earlier responses to the questions around the role and focus of the participants, many participants identified family notices as being very useful for family history research. Shipping lists, social columns, obituaries, and court reports were also mentioned in terms of their value for family history and local history research. One respondent said the court news was useful as their family members turn up there unfortunately often! Another participant elaborated on the value of social columns and shipping lists as follows:

A really useful source of information about people and their movements. In days when overseas travel or even travel between towns and cities was not common, these columns are useful to track people of some social standing to find out what they are doing, where they have come from, where they are going, and who they are meeting. I would include shipping news in this, especially in earlier days when lists of paying passengers was included.

Editorials and opinion pieces were described as helpful when wanting to get a sense of community feeling about a particular issue and similarly letters to the editor were identified as useful for gauging public opinion on a matter. Reports of meetings and events such as parliamentary or council proceedings, building openings, or sporting events, were described as very useful by users of Papers Past for professional or academic research.

Participants were then asked to consider how useful it would be if they could search Papers Past by genre and topic, either independently or in combination with a keyword search. Table 4 shows the results for a question in which the participants ranked the three search options with the most useful at the top and the least at the bottom. Perhaps unsurprisingly, because users are already familiar with keywords and the concept of topic is reasonably unambiguous, genre was ranked third by 78% of the participants, with 94% considering keyword to be most useful. However, almost a quarter of participants ranked genre in first or second place showing that, at least for a subset of users, filtering by genre is perceived as useful, particularly in combination with keyword, topic and other existing filtering options such as year or newspaper title.

Search by genre e.g., find all Letters to the Editor or Poetry

div.p: A subsequent open-ended question invited participants to comment further on the usefulness of these search options alone or in combination. Again, there was a great deal of variety in the 91 responses with some participants saying that keyword searching would be all they would ever need and others saying genre and topic would be useful, but pointing out that they would want to understand how these worked to ensure they were not missing anything important in the results. In particular, family history researchers who were focused on searching for people and places could not see much benefit in being able to limit searches by genre. However, in response to previous questions, several had commented on the fact that it would be useful to limit searches to family notices, certain types of reports, or obituaries. The answers here may therefore point to the difficulty of conceptualising how this type of search might work if it is not something the respondent is already familiar with. Most participants who saw the value in genre and topic filters identified that the three would be useful in combination in order to target different levels of detail, for example:

The genre search could be really useful as sometimes Letters to the Editor aren’t headlined as such. A keyword search could allow more specificity. A topic search would be useful where research is wanted on a very general topic.

Adding the ability to filter a keyword search by topic and/or genre could be useful in reducing the number of irrelevant searches. It would be more useful if you could tell it to ignore certain topics, e.g. don’t return any sports results.

div.head: Exploring users’ recognition and vocabulary of article genres
div.p: For genres to be useful for filtering and discovering information in an online collection, the taxonomy of terms used to describe them, also known as the genre palette, has to make sense and be recognisable to the people using it . As described above, 24 historical newspaper article genres were named by the survey participants and the genres they identified align closely with the high frequency genre terms in the previously prepared inventory of newspaper article genres. It is also fair to assume that if the survey participants were presented with examples of certain genres they had not mentioned, such as horoscope, they would easily be able to name them. The exception is probably the squib, which Onion describes as short pieces of filler that contained odd and compelling little stories to distract from the serious news of the day . The noun squib has 20 meanings listed in the Oxford English Dictionary. The closest to Onion's usage is: A smart gird or hit; a sharp scoff or sarcasm; a short composition of a satirical and witty character; a lampoon . The earliest evidence of this usage is given as c.1525 .

The case of the squib highlights much of what makes genre classification such a difficult, but also such an interesting, problem. As Santini et al. state, Genres are historical entities, they develop over time, and in response to social, cultural and technological contexts. Existing genres may simply go out of fashion, or undergo transformation . That is certainly the case for the squib, which is not a style of article today’s newspaper reader is likely to be familiar with. As Karlgren argues, genre requires a bidirectionality between reader and author:

When the character of text in a typical communicative situation is formed by or based on the bidirectional flow of authors' expectations on their audiences and that or those audiences' expectations on likely behaviour on the part of the authors they are reading, those items, or that family of items, constitute a genre.

The social, cultural, and technological contexts in which those shared expectations between squib authors and their audiences once flowed are now very distant from our own. Therefore, we cannot expect to fully recognise and understand the squib as a genre in the way its contemporary readers did. Still, it is a distinct form (the example shown in Figure 8 might reasonably be described as a squib, or a squib column) that readers browsing the nineteenth-century newspapers on Papers Past will inevitably encounter and which some users might want to specifically search for (or exclude). It is helpful, then, to give this family of articles a name and to explore the possibility of being able to automatically classify them based on certain distinctive features.

div.p: This leads to the last major section of the survey, in which participants were shown ten examples of Papers Past articles and asked to select from a list of 13 genres the one that best described the article (Other could also be selected and elaborated on). The participants could also enter one or more words to describe the topic of the article. The articles (which can be seen in Figure 9) had mostly been selected as difficult examples in order to test the relevance of the provided genre terms to Papers Past users and identify potential alternatives. The results of the genre selection exercise are shown in Table 5.

table.head: Participant genre selections for the ten example articles. The most selected genre for each article is highlighted in green.

div.p: The squib shown in Figure 8 is Article 8. The term Squib was not provided in the list of available genres in order to minimise confusion and avoid participants selecting terms they were unfamiliar with. The intention was to explore the fit of the given well-known genre terms with the example articles and to elicit the participants’ own choice of terms as alternatives. Article 8 was most often labelled as Humour, but less than half of the respondents (44%) made this selection. List and Opinion were also selected by 10% and 9% of respondents respectively, and it is easy to see why they were chosen. Other was selected by 16% of respondents and the suggestions here mainly include variations of Social and Gossip, as well as Snippets, Miscellany, Tidbits, Chat, or the article title, Table Talk. Many of these terms were also repeated in the suggested topics for this article, along with Politics, Tittle Tattle, and Random. In commenting on the distinguishing features of the article, several respondents noted the unfamiliarty of the article type for today’s reader:

This is another example of a form of journalism which has now practically vanished from our mass media, and is therefore mildly interesting for that reason alone. It consists of one-sentence mentions of people and issues of the day, typically without naming names so as to keep within the libel laws. Almost always worthless from the perspective of historical research.
I am familiar with Table Talk and have been puzzled by it. But it's the fact I can't understand it that lead me to understand it’s gossipy humour.
This is a weird one because nothing resembling this genre exists any more. Having seen hundreds of these I can decipher it, but without context the paragraphs are hard to interpret.

While the responses for every example article cannot be discussed here, the genre and topic selections and the comments from respondents in this section of the survey provide useful insights into the subjectivity of genre (and to a lesser extent topic), which align with the findings of user studies of web genres . The responses also reveal genres where there is a strong shared understanding (e.g., Letter, News, and Fiction) and those which are more subjective, unfamiliar, and difficult to classify (e.g., Opinion, Humour, and Report).

Finally, participants were asked to reflect on the task described above, indicating Yes or No to the question of whether they were uncertain about any of the genres they selected and commenting on why particular examples were difficult. Out of 123 respondents, 78% said they were uncertain about some of their genre selections. The subjective nature of assigning topics was also noted, as in this response:

Some took a bit of thinking to determine which genre was the best fit. The assigning of topics was quite difficult because it is quite subjective and we each have different backgrounds, knowledge, experience, perceptions, etc. that inform our choices.

Several respondents highlighted the Feature genre as being particularly difficult, with one participant stating, it seemed most equivalent to what I would have thought of as a news item. Other common challenges were a perceived ambiguity of Report, the fact that many of the articles had elements of several genres, and the difficulty of interpreting the genre of historical articles without additional context.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: The survey participants are highly engaged Papers Past users, with 91% using the newspaper collection at least monthly. Their feedback provides valuable, in-depth detail on how Papers Past is used, which search and filter features are most valued, and how they view the concepts of genre and topic in relation to historical newspaper articles.

The survey results confirmed the significance of family history research as a focus for users of digitised historical newspaper collections with 35% of respondents using Papers Past for this purpose either alone or in combination with other research activities. However, the survey respondents had a range of roles, including academics, archaeologists, archivists, professional historians, genealogists, authors, and other researchers with a variety of information needs and search strategies. Consistent with previous research was the reliance on simple keyword search (97% frequent use) and standard filters for date (92%) and region (80%), while advanced search features such as proximity search and wildcards were rarely used. The reliance on simple keyword search and minimal use of advanced search filters may be because users do not see a need for them, but it may also be because they are simply not aware of them. This was the case for some respondents who suggested search or interface features which already exist.

The survey results also show that genre and topic related filtering options would be of value to at least a portion of Papers Past users, and they are likely to be of similar interest to users of other digitised historical newspaper collections which do not currently provide filters for fine-grained article types. Genres of particular interest include letters to the editor, family notices, and shipping lists. However, the survey has also shown that the meaning of genre in relation to article types is not necessarily well understood by users of a historical newspaper collection and other terms such as article type may be more suitable for this audience. In addition, many historical newspaper articles do not neatly fit a single genre label, regardless of how that label is defined.

These findings contribute to longstanding and ongoing discussions in the literature related to genre as a search facet. As noted earlier, Crowston and Kwasnik recommend an initial descriptive phase in exploring genre as a facet for information retrieval, in which a target user group’s vocabulary and understanding of genre is investigated . This study provides an empirical case study of a digitised historical newspaper collection revealing where shared understanding exists and where perceptions of genre among users diverge. The high level of uncertainty expressed by participants when it came to assigning genres to example articles aligns with the findings of genre-related user studies from other domains such as web genre recognition and supports Karlgren’s argument that genre relies on a shared understanding between the author and reader . The strong agreement amongst survey participants for genres such as Letter, News, and Fiction shows that a core set of familiar and well-understood newspaper article genres exists, which could form the basis of a useful classification and retrieval schema. This aligns with Bowker and Star’s observation that while perfect classification schemes do not exist in the real world, pragmatically designed systems based on the shared understanding of a specific user group can be highly effective .

In terms of general limitations of the survey, the respondents were targeted and self-selected and another group of respondents, selected in a different way, may have different responses or preferences. In addition, the questions about genre and topic were very challenging for some respondents. This could reflect the inherent complexity and ambiguity of these concepts but could also indicate limitations in how the questions were framed. The intentional selection of ambiguous example articles is reflected in the high level of uncertainty reported (78%). This ambiguity annoyed some participants who may have perceived the task as having pre-determined correct answers which they wanted to get right.

Despite these limitations, the survey provides a detailed picture of how an engaged group of users search, interact with, and understand the content of a digitised historical newspaper collection. The findings contribute to our understanding of article types in digitised historical newspapers, and the vocabulary that today’s users adopt to describe them. The study also demonstrates that, while users may not always describe their information needs in terms of genre, they nonetheless have clear expectations about the types of articles they are searching for in historical newspapers.
